Question 37. Triple factorization is not sufficientOriginal/course-derived mathematical problem · individually revised answerConstructed counterexample for CMU Chapter 2, Exercise 2.15On eight equal atoms, let  A=B={1,2,3,4}  and  C={1,5,6,7}. Check the full triple product and a failed pair condition.
Read the complete construction, calculation and checksCheck the subfamilies instead of only the largest intersection. In eight equal atoms, take  A=B={1,2,3,4}  and  C={1,5,6,7}. All three marginal probabilities are one half. Their full intersection is only atom 1 and has probability one eighth, agreeing with  (1/2)3.
Nevertheless  A∩B=A  has probability one half instead of the product one quarter. Hence full-family factorization holds while the pair condition fails. Mutual independence requires both the triple equation and all the pair equations; the full intersection alone is insufficient. The three positive marginals and complete explicit sets ensure that this is a genuine finite model rather than a boundary trick. Checking both equalities numerically is essential when proposing a counterexample: a plausible description that fails its own advertised equality proves nothing about the intended implication.
Eight equal atoms: the repaired triple-only example1Mass 1/8AB and C2Mass 1/8AB only3Mass 1/8AB only4Mass 1/8AB only5Mass 1/8C only6Mass 1/8C only7Mass 1/8C only8Mass 1/8NeitherThis problem: A and B coincide on atoms 1 through 4; C contains atoms 1,5,6,7. All three marginals are one half and the triple mass is one eighth. The AB intersection is one half, so mutual independence fails.
